chapter_title: Debugging Smart Contracts and Transaction Analysis

screens.title: Debugging Smart Contracts and Transaction Analysis
screens.subtitle: Practical techniques with Hardhat: logging, tracing, debugging, and gas reporting

narration.text: In this chapter we'll learn how to find and fix bugs in Solidity contracts using the tools Hardhat provides. You will see how to add runtime logging to Solidity with Hardhat's console dot log, how to read transaction traces and stack traces to pinpoint which contract and call caused a failure, and how to use the Hardhat debugger to step through execution when you need a finer view. We'll also cover interpreting common runtime errors like out of gas, invalid opcode, and the Panic codes for arithmetic failures, and how gas reporting helps you optimize contract functions. Along the way you'll work through a short lab that starts with a failing token transfer and uses strategic logs and test runs to reveal and fix an incorrect require check. This matters because smart contracts are immutable on chain and every transaction consumes gas. Efficient debugging reduces time to fix, increases safety, and lowers cost for users. By the end you'll be able to approach a failing test, add targeted logs or a breakpoint, and read the trace to find the root cause.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical abilities that shorten debugging cycles and reduce costly mistakes. First, you'll be able to use Hardhat's console dot log in Solidity to print variable values and execution checkpoints while running local tests, giving immediate insight into contract state before a revert. Second, you'll learn to read transaction traces and stack traces so you can identify the specific contract and function call that produced an error, which is crucial in multi-contract systems. Third, you'll be able to use Hardhat's built-in debugger to pause execution, inspect local variables and storage, and step through the EVM execution when logs and traces aren't enough. Fourth, you'll understand gas reporting and how to run tests with a gas reporter to identify expensive functions to optimize. Each objective includes a small example or mnemonic to tie the skill to a real action: print, trace, step, and measure. These skills together let you move from symptom to root cause with confidence and avoid deploying easily preventable runtime failures.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical lab and safety
screens.subtitle: What you will practice and safe habits to adopt

narration.text: This second objectives slide ties the skills to a hands-on lab and to safe development habits. You'll walk through a failing token transfer test, add targeted prints to the transfer function, run tests to see the console output, and use the information to fix an incorrect require check. This lab reinforces both the mechanics of adding logs and the habit of testing all revert paths. In addition, you'll learn safety checks: do not rely on console logging for production debugging, and always inspect revert reasons and gas usage before deploying. You'll practice verifying the fix by running the test suite again and enabling gas reporting to ensure that changes did not accidentally increase cost. The goals are to build a tight feedback loop—add logs, run tests, read traces, step when needed—and to adopt the discipline of testing every edge case and reading compiler warnings. These practices reduce time-to-fix and lower risk when deploying immutable contracts.

screens.title: Why smart contract debugging is unique
screens.subtitle: Immutability, determinism, and gas constraints change the game

narration.text: Debugging smart contracts is different from debugging standard apps because contracts run in an immutable, deterministic environment where every instruction costs gas. Unlike a web app where you can attach a live debugger and change state, once a contract is deployed on chain you cannot change its code. That constraint raises the stakes: mistakes cost money and can require complex migrations. Determinism means the EVM will produce the same results for the same inputs and state, which is helpful when reproducing bugs locally but also means you must recreate the same state to reproduce a failure. Gas limits act as both a resource and a failure mode: running out of gas causes a revert without reaching later assertions. A common misconception is that on-chain debugging is impossible — it isn't. You can reproduce transactions locally, add development-only logs, and trace execution in an instrumented environment. For example, a test-run that triggers a revert can be replayed on Hardhat Network, giving the same trace and console output you saw in CI. The practical takeaway is to design repeatable test scenarios, add targeted logs to reveal state, and use traces and step-through debugging when logs are insufficient. Which of your usual debugging habits will you adapt when a function's execution cost is limited by gas?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Smart contract debugging focuses on reproducible local environments, targeted logs, and careful gas-aware inspection because deployed contracts are immutable and costly to fix.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Why smart contract debugging is unique
What makes it different
Immutability, deterministic replayability, and gas as a failure mode are the main differences developers must plan for.
  • Design reproducible test states to replay failing transactions locally.
  • Use development-only logging to inspect values during test runs.
  • Treat out-of-gas as a functional failure to be diagnosed like a logic bug.
Key Takeaway

Prepare reproducible local scenarios and prefer targeted logs and traces before attempting on-chain fixes.

Concrete example
A failing transfer test that reverts with a generic message can be reproduced on Hardhat Network. Adding a few development logs reveals the last computed balances and shows which condition failed before the revert, enabling a quick fix and verification.
Common misconception
Some developers believe production logs are sufficient. In reality console logs exist only in development; once deployed you must use traces, events, and explorers to diagnose runs.
Why it matters
Immutable code and gas costs make small bugs expensive. Fast local debugging and gas-aware fixes reduce both time and monetary cost.

screens.title: Hardhat's console.log in Solidity
screens.subtitle: Add development-only prints to view values during local tests

narration.text: Hardhat provides a development-only console printing utility for Solidity that behaves like a quick probe into contract state during local test runs. To use it you import the helper into your contract and then call the print function at key points inside functions. This is especially useful when a test triggers a revert and you want to see the last variable values and execution path. For example, in a constructor or a transfer function you can log the sender, the recipient, and the current balances just before the require that may fail. When you run npx hardhat test locally the printed lines appear in your terminal and help you infer which condition caused the failure. A common mistake is leaving prints in code intended for deployment — console logs are for development only and will not work on a live network. Another pitfall is scattering too many logs; instead prefer a few strategic prints that show inputs, key intermediate results, and outputs. Practice: add three logs in a failing transfer function showing the sender, recipient, and sender balance, run tests, and read the terminal output to identify the incorrect balance check. What single variable will you log first?

keyIdea.title: Console log usage
keyIdea.text: Import the Hardhat console helper and add a few targeted prints in functions to reveal the values leading up to a revert during test runs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Hardhat console.log
Code example
Import the console helper and place prints at strategic points to reveal values.
// contracts/BuggyContract.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

import "hardhat/console.sol"; // Import console.log

contract BuggyContract {
  uint public value;
  address public owner;

  constructor() {
    owner = msg.sender;
    value = 100;
  }

  function setValue(uint _newValue) public {
    // console.log("Attempting to set value to:", _newValue); // Debugging line
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can set value");
    if (_newValue > 200) {
      console.log("New value is too high!");
      revert("Value cannot exceed 200");
    }
    value = _newValue;
    console.log("Value successfully set to:", value);
  }
}
How it helps
See runtime values to understand why a require or revert happened without pausing execution.
Common mistake
Leaving console prints in code intended for deployment — they only work in Hardhat local environment.
Terminal example
When a test hits the code above, you'll see the printed messages in your test run output, helping you trace execution.
Check your understanding
If a transfer reverts, which three values should you print first? Think inputs, relevant balances, and a key intermediate result.
Key Takeaway

Use console dot log for quick, development-only insights; prefer a few strategic prints instead of many scattered logs.

screens.title: Using console.log to find a bug
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step approach for the VulnerableToken transfer bug

narration.text: When you have a failing transfer test, a short, repeatable process with console prints helps you find the bug fast. Start by writing a minimal test that reproduces the failure and run it to confirm the revert. Next, add three targeted prints in the transfer function: the sender address, the recipient address, and the sender balance before the require. Run the tests again and observe the terminal output to see whether the balance matches your expectation. The lab's provided hint notes an incorrect require check that examines the recipient balance instead of the sender's. Seeing printed balances will reveal that the sender's balance is lower than expected while the recipient's is irrelevant, pointing directly to the misplaced check. After you identify the faulty line, change the require to check the sender's balance, then re-run all tests to ensure the fix didn't break other scenarios. A common misconception is expecting console prints to change execution timing or state; they only report values and do not alter logic. This process repeats well: reproduce, print, interpret, fix, verify. Using console.log to find a bug means reproduce the failure, add targeted logs for inputs and a key state value, interpret the output, fix the faulty check, and verify with tests.. In practical terms, a step-by-step approach for the vulnerabletoken transfer bug. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Transaction trace vs stack trace
screens.subtitle: When to use each and what they reveal

narration.text: Transaction traces and stack traces are complementary diagnostic tools. A transaction trace records the sequence of internal calls, opcodes executed, and value transfers that occurred during a transaction, helping you see the call chain across multiple contracts. This is essential when your failing test involves interactions between contracts or libraries. A stack trace, on the other hand, lists the active function calls at the point of failure and helps you inspect the sequence of function frames that led to the revert. Use a trace when you need the full call graph and state changes; use a stack when you want the immediate sequence of function calls and which source lines corresponded to the revert. A common misconception is that a trace will always show the exact variable values — traces show call and opcode-level detail, but to see high-level variables you often need console prints or the debugger. For example, a trace may reveal that Contract A called Contract B which called Contract C where the revert happened; the stack trace will show the function chain that led into Contract C. Knowing which tool to pick will reduce the time spent chasing the wrong contract.

keyIdea.title: Trace vs Stack
keyIdea.text: Use transaction traces to view the full call graph and stack traces to inspect the active sequence of function calls at failure time.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Trace vs Stack
Transaction Trace
Shows all internal calls, value movements, and low-level operations performed during a transaction.
  • Useful across multi-contract interactions to locate which contract changed state.
  • Does not always show high-level variable names; pair with logs or debugger for clarity.
Stack Trace
Lists active function frames and the sequence of function calls at the point of failure.
  • Helps identify the source line and function where a revert was triggered.
  • Best when you already suspect a contract and need the exact failing frame.
Key Takeaway

Traces show the full call path. Stacks show the active function chain at failure. Use both together for multi-contract bugs.

screens.title: Hardhat built-in debugger
screens.subtitle: Set breakpoints and step through transaction execution

narration.text: When logs and traces are insufficient to reveal the state that led to a failure, the Hardhat debugger lets you step through execution and inspect variables and storage at breakpoints. You invoke the debugger by adding a debugger statement in your test code or by running Hardhat in debug mode to replay a failing transaction. Once paused, you can examine local variables, contract storage, and the call stack to see the exact state at a given instruction. This is especially useful when a condition depends on several computed values or when you need to inspect memory and storage layout. A misconception is that the debugger will feel like a full IDE experience; it is command-line oriented and focused on EVM-level state rather than high-level language niceties. Use the debugger when you need a reproducible transaction replay and precise inspection — for instance, to confirm that an intermediate arithmetic result overflows or that storage slots hold unexpected values. After identifying the problem, remove debugger statements and re-run tests to confirm the fix. Hardhat built-in debugger means use hardhat's debugger to step through a replayed transaction, inspect locals and storage, and confirm the precise state that caused a revert.. In practical terms, set breakpoints and step through transaction execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Interpreting common Solidity errors
screens.subtitle: Revert reasons, out of gas, invalid opcode, and Panic codes

narration.text: Interpreting Solidity runtime errors quickly helps you narrow the cause of a failing transaction. A revert or require with a reason string is usually explicit: it tells you which contract assertion failed. 'Out of gas' indicates the transaction ran out of gas before completing, which can be caused by an infinite loop, an unexpectedly expensive operation, or simply not supplying enough gas. 'Invalid opcode' or 'Bad jump destination' are less common and often point to corrupted bytecode or misuse of low-level calls; they require deeper inspection. Solidity also surfaces Panic codes for particular runtime failures, for example Panic code 0x11 indicates an arithmetic overflow or underflow in contexts without SafeMath protections, while 0x12 indicates division by zero. Since Solidity 0.8+ has built-in overflow checks, the classic overflow panic happens less often, but you should still be aware of arithmetic pitfalls. A helpful practice is to pair error messages with console prints and traces — the message points you to a failing assertion, prints show variable values, and the trace identifies which contract and function produced the message. Always cover revert paths in tests to avoid untested surprises in production.

keyIdea.title: Error interpretation
keyIdea.text: Use the revert reason as the first clue, then consult prints and traces; Panic codes map to specific runtime faults like arithmetic errors or division by zero.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Interpreting common Solidity errors
Common runtime errors
revert / require
Usually explicit reason strings tell you which assertion failed; use this with logs to find variable values.
Out of gas
Transaction ran out of gas before completion; check loops and gas-heavy computations.
Invalid opcode / Bad jump
Less common; may indicate low-level call misuse or corrupted bytecode.
Panic codes
Numeric codes like 0x11 or 0x12 map to specific runtime faults (overflow, division by zero).
Concrete example
If a function returns Panic 0x11, suspect arithmetic operations or indexing beyond bounds; add prints for operands to confirm.
Misconception
Assuming a generic 'revert' has no useful information. Even a generic revert can be paired with logs to reveal the failing condition.
Key Takeaway

Read the revert reason first, then confirm with logs or debugger and consult traces to find the failing contract in multi-contract flows.

screens.title: VulnerableToken: spot the intentional bug
screens.subtitle: Review the buggy transfer implementation and identify the wrong check

narration.text: The VulnerableToken contract provided in the lab intentionally contains a single incorrect require condition to teach targeted debugging. The contract stores balances in a mapping and assigns the initial supply to the deployer. The transfer function intends to ensure the sender has enough balance before subtracting the amount, but the require statement incorrectly tests the recipient's balance instead. This leads to unexpected reverts even when the sender has sufficient funds. When you add prints for msg. sender, _to, _value, and balanceOf[msg. sender] you will see that the sender balance is insufficient or that the wrong balance is being checked, confirming the bug. The fix is straightforward: change the require to inspect balanceOf[msg. sender] rather than balanceOf[_to]. A common misconception is to assume arithmetic or event emission causes the revert; in this case the logic check is wrong. After applying the corrected condition, re-run the failing test and ensure it passes and that no other tests regressed. VulnerableToken: spot the intentional bug means the require statement checks the wrong account's balance; printing sender and balances during tests exposes the incorrect condition immediately.. In practical terms, review the buggy transfer implementation and identify the wrong check. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bug identification
keyIdea.text: The require statement checks the wrong account's balance; printing sender and balances during tests exposes the incorrect condition immediately.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › VulnerableToken bug
Buggy transfer function
// contracts/VulnerableToken.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

import "hardhat/console.sol";

contract VulnerableToken {
  string public name = "BuggyToken";
  string public symbol = "BGT";
  uint public totalSupply;
  mapping(address => uint) public balanceOf;

  constructor(uint _initialSupply) {
    totalSupply = _initialSupply;
    balanceOf[msg.sender] = _initialSupply;
  }

  function transfer(address _to, uint _value) public returns (bool success) {
    // THE BUG IS HERE!
    require(balanceOf[_to] >= _value, "Insufficient sender balance"); // This is the bug!

    balanceOf[msg.sender] -= _value;
    balanceOf[_to] += _value;

    emit Transfer(msg.sender, _to, _value);
    return true;
  }

  event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint value);
}
What to print
Add prints for msg.sender, _to, _value, and balanceOf[msg.sender] to observe real values during the failing test.
Hint
The require checks the recipient's balance instead of the sender's. Correct the mapping index to msg.sender.
Key Takeaway

Targeted prints reveal the wrong variable quickly; fixes should be verified by re-running tests and checking gas impact.

screens.title: Gas reporting and optimization
screens.subtitle: Measure function costs and prioritize optimization

narration.text: Gas reporting is essential because every on-chain operation consumes gas which directly affects user cost. Hardhat's gas reporter plugin summarizes gas used by each function during tests, helping you identify hot spots and prioritize optimization work. To use it, enable the reporter in your test run and review the per-function breakdown: look for functions with unexpectedly high gas relative to their importance. Optimizations may include reducing storage writes, batching operations, or simplifying loops. A frequent error is optimizing prematurely; always measure first. Another common mistake is focusing only on a single function without considering how often it's called; a slightly expensive function called thousands of times can cost more overall than a very expensive function called rarely. After making changes, re-run tests with the reporter to confirm improvements and ensure no regressions in correctness. Use gas reporting alongside unit testing to keep a balance between safety and efficiency before any deployment. Gas reporting and optimization means run tests with a gas reporter to find expensive functions, measure improvements after refactors, and prioritize optimizations by usage frequency.. In practical terms, measure function costs and prioritize optimization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gas reporting
keyIdea.text: Run tests with a gas reporter to find expensive functions, measure improvements after refactors, and prioritize optimizations by usage frequency.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Gas reporting
Why measure gas
Gas reporting shows the real cost of functions and helps you target optimizations that reduce user fees.
Insights from the reporter
  • Which functions consume the most gas per call.
  • How refactors change gas consumption.
  • Trade-offs between storage writes and computation.
Run example
npx hardhat test --gas-reporter
Practical tip
Optimize hotspots that are called frequently; measure before and after each change to verify real gains.
Key Takeaway

Measure first, prioritize by call frequency, and re-run the reporter after refactors to validate improvements.

screens.title: Pitfalls and safety notes
screens.subtitle: Warnings developers often ignore during debugging

narration.text: There are several recurring mistakes that slow debugging and increase risk. First, ignoring compiler warnings is dangerous; many warnings hint at potential runtime issues. Second, relying solely on a single failing test without covering all revert paths can leave hidden bugs in untested scenarios. Third, leaving console logs in code intended for deployment is a misuse; console logs only work in the development environment and should never be relied on on-chain. Fourth, optimizing without measuring can lead to wasted effort or subtle correctness regressions. Finally, misreading traces or assuming the top-level failing contract is the true root cause is a common error in multi-contract systems — use stack traces to inspect the sequence and console prints to inspect values. To avoid these pitfalls, adopt a practice of running the full test suite after fixes, turning on gas reporting before major refactors, and pairing prints with traces and the debugger. A concise safety checklist prevents many otherwise costly mistakes in live deployments. Pitfalls and safety notes means don't ignore warnings, test all revert paths, remove development logs before deploy, and measure before optimizing.. In practical terms, warnings developers often ignore during debugging. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls
keyIdea.text: Don't ignore warnings, test all revert paths, remove development logs before deploy, and measure before optimizing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Pitfalls and safety
Common mistakes
  • Ignoring compiler warnings — these often point to risky patterns you should fix before testing.
  • Testing only the happy path — make sure revert paths are covered to avoid surprises.
  • Leaving dev logs in production code — logs won't help on-chain and may be misleading.
Safety checklist
  1. Run the full test suite after any fix.
  2. Enable gas reporting before and after refactors.
  3. Use targeted logs and remove them before deployment.
  4. Pair traces with prints and debugger for multi-contract issues.
Warning

A quick patch without full verification can introduce regressions. Always verify correctness and gas after changes.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the main concepts. First, Hardhat's console dot log gives fast, development-only prints that reveal inputs and intermediate values during test runs. Second, transaction traces and stack traces are complementary: traces show the full call graph and state changes, and stack traces show the active function sequence at the failure point. Third, interpret Solidity error messages carefully — revert reasons point to failed assertions, out of gas signals resource exhaustion, invalid opcode indicates low-level failure, and Panic codes map to specific runtime faults like arithmetic errors. Together these tools let you move from symptom to root cause in a reproducible local environment. Keep the habit of targeted logging, covering revert paths in tests, and using the debugger for deep inspection when logs and traces are insufficient. Finally, measure gas usage with a reporter before optimizing. These practices shorten debug cycles and reduce the risk of costly production fixes.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick reference
screens.subtitle: Compact reminders for debugging and analysis

narration.text: Keep these three compact reminders top of mind. First, prints are your quickest probe: use Hardhat's console dot log to reveal inputs and immediate state during local tests. Second, traces and stacks guide you to the faulty contract and function in multi-contract interactions; use traces for the call graph and stack traces to see the active frames. Third, always measure gas and verify fixes: enable gas reporting to understand cost impact before you finalize changes. These three practices — print, trace, measure — form a lightweight workflow that finds most bugs and prevents cost surprises. As you practice the lab, try to apply this pattern and ask: did my fix change gas consumption, and did I cover all revert paths in tests? Key Concepts — Quick reference means three practical steps to debug effectively: add targeted prints, read traces to locate the failing contract, and measure gas to assess cost impact.. In practical terms, compact reminders for debugging and analysis. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
